topic: AirPods health warning for heart patients
headline_marked: [[AirPods can trigger magnet mode]] in pacemakers and defibrillators, studies show
headline: AirPods can trigger magnet mode in pacemakers and defibrillators, studies show
summary: Studies reveal magnetic fields from AirPods and other devices can temporarily disrupt cardiovascular implants. The FDA advises keeping electronics at least six inches away from CIDs.
details: Cardiologists have long warned about the risks smartphones, headphones, and other consumer devices pose towards cardiovascular implantable devices (CIDs). Concerns revolve around the magnetic fields these devices emit.

These magnetic fields can inadvertently trigger a magnet-safe mode on defibrillators and pacemakers. This mode potentially prevents them from detecting tachycardia or other cardiovascular irregularities, which can have major consequences.

Modern CIDs are designed to automatically switch into this mode when near strong magnetic fields, ensuring patient safety during magnet-intensive medical procedures like MRIs. While CIDs are designed to return to normal after the magnetic field is removed, even a temporary disruption can be critical.

CIDs typically switch into magnet mode when they encounter a magnetic induction field of 10 Gauss or more. The mass proliferation of small rare-earth magnets across consumer electronics has begun to pose unique risks to medical implants.

A 2022 study published in Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology found that the magnetic fields of Apple's AirPods are strong enough to trigger magnetic modes in implanted cardiovascular devices. The study also noted similar effects from devices like iPhone 12 Pro Max, Apple Pencil, and Microsoft Surface Pen.

These reports do not necessarily preclude those with heart conditions from using AirPods. Apple's support page recommends that customers keep AirPods and other electronic devices at least 6 inches away from their cardiovascular device.

The FDA offers several suggestions for consumers with CIDs when handling electronic devices. Always keep electronic devices at least six inches from a CID, meaning avoiding front shirt pockets for phones or AirPods.

If concerned, the FDA suggests consulting your home monitoring system to ensure your CID is operating properly. Those experiencing dizziness, loss of consciousness, or any other heart-related symptoms should consult with their physician immediately.

topic: Fitbit Air AI fitness tracker review
headline_marked: [[Fitbit Air launches for $100]] with an AI Coach and screen-less design
headline: Fitbit Air launches for $100 with an AI Coach and screen-less design
summary: The new screen-less fitness tracker offers an AI Coach for personalized plans, but accessing its full potential requires a Google Health Premium subscription starting at $10/month.
details: The Fitbit Air is now available for $100 through Google's online store, Amazon, Best Buy, and other retailers. This highly anticipated wearable features a back-to-basics, screen-less design and an innovative AI Coach.

It weighs just 11 grams, making it a low-distraction, easy-to-wear fitness tracker that disappears on your wrist. This makes it ideal for 24-hour wear, including sleep tracking, without being noticeable.

The device comes standard with a recycled polyester Performance Loop Band, available in Obsidian, Lavender, Berry, and Fog, matching the Google Pixel 10a colors. Optional silicone Active Bands ($35) and polyurethane Elevated Modern Bands ($50) are also available.

To fully utilize the Google Health AI Coach for custom workout plans and data interpretation, users need a Google Health Premium subscription. This costs $10 per month or $100 per year, or is included in the Google AI Pro subscription.

The Fitbit Air competes with other screen-less trackers like the Oura Ring 4 and Whoop MG, both of which also require subscriptions. It also offers an alternative to smartwatches such as the Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 and Apple Watch Series 11.

The device connects to the Google Health app, which has replaced the older Fitbit and Google Fit apps. The app displays key data points like steps, readiness, sleep, and cardio goals, along with detailed vitals such as breathing rate and heart rate variability.

Unlike smartwatches, the Fitbit Air does not deliver notifications or vibrate unnecessarily, though it can be set to vibrate for alarms. Its simple design also makes it suitable for wearing alongside a traditional mechanical watch.

The reviewer found no issues with connecting the Fitbit Air to Google Health, noting its modern app design. The device's comfort and customization options contribute to its appeal as a versatile fitness companion.
